title: Powered patient support apparatus

claims.text: A patient support apparatus (20) comprising: a base (22); a powered wheel (24a) and a steerable wheel (24b); a patient support deck (30) supported by said base (22), said patient support deck (30) adapted to support a patient; a first motor (54) adapted to provide power to said powered wheel (24a); a second motor (56) adapted to steer said steerable wheel (24b), characterized in that the apparatus further includes a force sensing system (50,52) adapted to detect both a direction and magnitude of forces exerted by a user and to determine a location of the applied forces relative to a reference location (90) on the patient support apparatus; and a controller (50) adapted to control said first and second motors (54, 56) in a manner that takes into account the magnitude, direction, and moment of the applied forces relative to the reference location, and to power the powered wheel (24a) and steer the steerable wheel (24b) in a manner that amplifies how the patient support apparatus would move if it were subjected to only the exerted forces.
The patient support apparatus (20) of claim 1 wherein said powered wheel (24a) and said steerable wheel (24b) are the same wheel (24c).

The patient support apparatus (20) of claim 1 further including a plurality of side rails (44), and wherein said force sensing system (50,52) includes a plurality of force sensors (52) mounted to said plurality of side rails (44).

The patient support apparatus (20) of claim 1 further including: a litter (28) supported on said base (22), said litter (28) adapted to support said patient support deck (30); and a force sensor (52) positioned to detect forces exerted in a generally horizontal orientation against said litter (28), said force sensor (52) configured to determine both a magnitude and direction of any forces exerted against said litter (28).

The patient support apparatus (20) of claim 1 further including a brake, wherein said controller (50) senses whether said brake is turned on or off, and if said brake is turned on, said controller (50) does not control said first and second motors (54, 56) based upon information from said force sensing system (50,52).

The patient support apparatus (20) of claim 1 wherein said force sensing system (50,52) includes a plurality of load cells adapted to detect both a magnitude and direction of a horizontal component of force applied by a user to said patient support apparatus (20).

The patient support apparatus (20) of claim 1 wherein said force sensing system (50,52) includes a first force sensor (52) and a second force sensor (52), both said first force sensor (52) and said second force sensor (52) configured to detect horizontal forces applied to said patient support apparatus (20) by a user; and wherein said controller (50) is adapted to steer said steerable wheel (24b) based at least partially upon a difference between a force sensed by said first force sensor (52) and a force sensed by said second force sensor (52).
The patient support apparatus (20) of claim 1 wherein said patient support apparatus (20) is one of a bed, stretcher, or cot.

The patient support apparatus (20) of claim 1 further including: a second steerable wheel (24b); a third motor (56) adapted to steer said second steerable wheel (24b); and wherein said controller (50) is adapted to control said third motor (56) based upon information received from said force sensing system (50,52).

The patient support apparatus (20) of claim 9 wherein said steerable wheel (24b) and said second steerable wheel (24b) are each located adjacent a corner of said base (22) of said patient support apparatus (20).

The patient support apparatus (20) of claim 9 wherein said controller (50) is adapted to be able to steer said steerable wheel (24b) and said second steerable wheel (24b) such that said patient support apparatus (20) is rotatable about a center of rotation that is positioned outside of a footprint of said patient support apparatus (20).

The patient support apparatus (20) of any preceding claim wherein said force sensing system (50,52) includes a force sensor positioned at a junction of a wheel and a mount for said wheel, said mount for said wheel being supported on said base (22); wherein said force sensor is adapted to detect both a direction and a magnitude of any horizontal force between said wheel and said wheel mount, and wherein said controller (50) steers said steerable wheel (24b) and powers said powered wheel (24a) in a manner that is based upon said magnitude and direction.

A method of controlling movement of a patient support apparatus (20) having a steerable wheel (24b) and a powered wheel (24a), said method comprising: providing a force sensing system (50, 52) on said patient support apparatus (20), said force sensing system (50, 52) adapted to detect a magnitude and direction of forces applied by a user to the patient support apparatus (20) and to determine a location of the applied forces relative to a reference location (90) on the patient support apparatus; providing a controller (50) on said patient support apparatus (20) adapted to control steering of said steerable wheel (24b) and to control power delivered to said powered wheel (24a), characterized by controlling said powered wheel (24a) and said steerable wheel (24a) in a manner that takes into account the magnitude, direction, and moment of the applied force relative to the reference location (90), and that amplifies how the patient support apparatus (20) would turn if it were subjected to only the applied force.

## Description

<u>BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION</u>
* [0001]

  The present invention relates to patient support apparatuses-such as, but not limited to, beds, stretchers, cots, operating tables, and the like-and more particularly to patient support apparatuses that have at least one powered wheel to assist in the movement of the patient support apparatus over a floor.
* [0002]

  Patient support apparatuses are used in hospitals, nursing homes, and other healthcare facilities for both supporting patients within a room or other location, as well as transporting patients between rooms and/or other locations. While most patient support apparatuses include one or more wheels that allow the support apparatus to be wheeled from the first location to the second location, the weight and bulk of the patient support apparatus-including the weight of the patient supported thereon, can make it difficult for a caregiver to manually wheel the support apparatus from one location to another. This can be especially difficult when there are inclines in the floors of the healthcare facility, or when there are long distances involved, or when the patient and/or the support apparatus are heavy. This difficulty can be further exacerbated when it is desirable to maneuver the patient support apparatus into, or through, areas with little excess clearance, such as in elevators, rooms, or corridors, or when turning the patient support apparatus around a corner, or steering it past obstacles.
* [0003]

  In the past, powered patient support apparatuses have been provided that include a powered wheel that is driven by a motor positioned on the patient support apparatus. One such example is shown in  [U.S. patent 6,752,224 issued to Hopper et al](/patent/US6752224) . In prior powered support apparatuses, the powered wheel responds to controls issued by a caregiver. In some instances, the caregiver controls the powered wheel by one or more handles positioned at an end of the patient support apparatus. When the caregiver pushes forward on the handle, the powered wheel powers the support apparatus forward. Conversely, when the caregiver pulls back on the handle, the powered wheel brakes or moves backward. A load cell, a potentiometer, or some other type of sensor may be used to sense the forward/backward pushing of the caregiver.  [US 2008/141459](/patent/US20080141459)  discloses a patient support apparatus operated by a user interface with switches.  JP 2000 016298  discloses a cargo carriage with a force sensor for measuring an operator's pushing force.  [DE 199 49 351](/patent/DE19949351)  discloses a wheel module with a drive motor and a steering motor in which one of the steering shaft or the drive shaft is hollow and rotatably receives the other shaft.
* [0004]

  A further powered patient support apparatus is disclosed in  [WO2012/055407A1](/patent/WO2012055407A1) .
* [0005]

  Despite the assistance of the powered wheel, prior art powered patient support apparatuses can still be difficult to use, and/or suffer from other disadvantages.
<u>SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION</u>
* [0006]

  The invention is defined by the claims. Accordingly, the various aspects of the present invention provide powered patient support apparatuses with improved controls and/or other features that make the powered support apparatus easier to use, steer, and/or control. In some aspects, the patient support apparatus of the present invention provides improved movement control by providing multiple touch points that enable the caregiver to move the apparatus in multiple directions. That is, the caregiver can be positioned virtually anywhere around the perimeter of the patient support apparatus and, without having to change position vis-à-vis the support apparatus, he or she can move the support apparatus in any direction. The patient support apparatuses include motorized steerable wheels that are steered in accordance with input from a user. The motor controls the steering of one or more wheels to match the direction in which the user wishes the patient control apparatus to move. The motorized steered wheels are the same as the powered wheels that move the support apparatus in one embodiment, while they are separate from the wheels that provide motive force to the support apparatus in another embodiment. By controlling not only the powered movement of the wheels, but also the steering of the wheels, a caregiver or other person moving the support apparatus is better able to control, steer, and/or move the support apparatus in tight spaces, around corners, and/or through narrow openings.
* [0007]

  A patient support apparatus is disclosed that includes a base, a patient support deck, a first motor, a second motor, a force sensing system, and a controller. The base includes a powered wheel and a steerable wheel. The support deck is supported by the base and is adapted to support a patient. The first motor provides power to the powered wheel, and the second motor provides powered steering assistance to the steerable wheel. The force sensing system is adapted to detect forces exerted by a user, and the controller is adapted to control the first and second motors based upon information received from the force sensing system.
* [0008]

  A patient support apparatus is disclosed that includes a base, a patient support deck, a first motor, a second motor, a user input, and a controller. The base includes a plurality of powered wheels and a plurality of steerable wheel. The patient support deck is supported by the base and is adapted to support a patient. The first motor is adapted to provide power to at least one of the powered wheels, and the second motor is adapted to steer at least one of the steerable wheels. The controller controls the first and second motors based upon information received from the user input whereby the first and second motors assist in moving and steering the patient support apparatus over a floor.
* [0009]

  In some embodiments, the powered wheel(s) and the steerable wheel(s) are the same wheel(s), while in other embodiments, they are different wheels. The force sensing system includes one or more force sensors that are mounted to one or more of the side rails of the patient support apparatus, or to other locations. In some embodiments, there is a single force sensor mounted per side rail, while in other embodiments, there are multiple force sensors mounted per side rail. Force sensors may also, or alternatively, be mounted the footboard and/or the headboard of the patient support apparatus, particularly if the patient support apparatus is a bed, or other apparatus having a headboard or footboard. Regardless of where they are mounted, the force sensors are adapted to determine both a magnitude and direction of force applied thereto, such that the controller steers the steerable wheel and powers the powered wheel in a manner that is based upon the magnitude and direction sensed by the force sensors.
* [0010]

  A litter is disclosed that is supported on the base that supports or includes the patient support deck. The force sensors are positioned to detect forces exerted in a generally horizontal orientation against the litter, wherein the controller uses the force sensor readings to determine both a magnitude and direction of the forces and to steer the steerable wheel and power the powered wheel in a manner that is based upon the determined magnitude and direction. In some embodiments, the force sensor is positioned at a junction of the litter and one or more height adjustment mechanisms that raise and lower the height of the litter, or the force sensor is positioned at the junction of one or more of the height adjustment mechanisms and the base. In still other embodiments, one or more force sensors are positioned at a junction of a wheel and a mount for the wheel, wherein the force sensor is adapted to detect both a direction and a magnitude of any horizontal force between the wheel and the wheel mount, and wherein the controller steers the steerable wheel and powers the powered wheel in a manner that is based upon the magnitude and direction detected by the force sensor.
* [0011]

  In some embodiments, the controller senses whether the brake is turned on or off. If the brake is turned on, the controller does not control the first and second motors, regardless of any forces sensed or any control signals provided by the user input. However, if the brake is turned off, then the controller is configured to automatically respond to any force readings or other manipulations of the user input that are intended to control the movement of the patient support apparatus.
* [0012]

  In any of the embodiments utilizing force sensors, the force sensors may be, or include, one or more load cells positioned in any of the locations described herein. Also, in any of the embodiments using force sensors, the controller uses the force sensor readings from multiple force sensors in order to determine how to steer and power the patient support apparatus. Depending upon the location of the force sensors and/or the configuration of the patient support apparatus, the controller computes the difference between force sensor readings, or sums and/or otherwise combines the readings from multiple force sensors, including, but not limited to, calculating moments of force created with respect to a center point or other reference on the support apparatus. In some instances, the multiple detected forces are forces exerted by each hand of a single caregiver, while in other instances the multiple detected forces are forces exerted by multiple caregivers on the patient support apparatus.
* [0013]

  The one or more steerable wheels may be located adjacent one or more of the corners of the patient support apparatus. In such instances, the powered wheel or wheels may be located interior from the corners, or they may also be located at one or more of the corners, or they may be the same wheels as the steerable wheels. Still further, in some embodiments, there are two powered wheels that are coaxially aligned and the steering is effectuated by rotating one of the wheels faster or slower than the other of the two coaxially aligned wheels.
* [0014]

  The steerable wheels are configured to allow the patient support apparatus to rotate about a center of rotation that is positioned outside of the footprint of the patient support apparatus. In embodiments where there are multiple steered wheels, one or more of the steered wheels may be controlled by a first motor while one or more of the other steered wheels may be controlled by a second motor that is independent of the first motor. In this manner, the wheels are able to be steered to have different orientations than each other, thereby allowing-at least in some embodiments-the support apparatus to be Ackermann steered. Such independent steering also allows-in some embodiments-tight cornering, particularly in situations where wheels at the forward end of the support apparatus are steered independently from wheels at the rearward end of the support apparatus.
* [0015]

  In any of the embodiments described herein, the patient support apparatus may be one of a bed, a stretcher, or a cot.
* [0016]

  In any of the embodiments described herein, the patient support apparatus is modifiable to further include one or more object sensors positioned thereon that detect the presence and/or location of nearby objects. The detection of such objects is used for collision avoidance or steering, as well as navigation and/or docking of the patient support apparatus. In some embodiments, the detection of objects influences not only the automatic steering of the support apparatus, but also the speed of the patient support apparatus. That is, depending upon the location of the detect object(s), the controller not only changes direction, but also change speeds. Indeed, in some embodiments, the controller is in communication with a brake or brakes such that the speed of the patient support apparatus is actively decelerated, if desired.
* [0017]

  A method is disclosed for controlling the movement of a patient support apparatus having a steerable wheel and a powered wheel. The method includes providing a user input on the patient support apparatus that is adapted to detect a magnitude and direction of desired movement of the patient support apparatus over a floor; providing a controller on the patient support apparatus that is adapted to control steering of the steerable wheel and to control the power delivered to the powered wheel; steering the steerable wheel in a manner based upon the direction of desired movement of the patient support apparatus; and supplying an amount of power to the powered wheel that is based upon the magnitude of the desired movement.
* [0018]

  The method further may include providing an object sensor positioned on the patient support apparatus, and steering the steerable wheel in a manner based both upon the desired movement of the patient support apparatus and information received from the object sensor. The steering may include steering the steerable wheel so as to avoid an object detected by the object sensor even if the user input detects a desired direction of movement that would otherwise lead to a collision with the detected object. In addition, or alternatively, the method may include steering a plurality of steerable wheels on the patient support apparatus based upon information received from the object sensor.
* [0019]

  The method may include providing a plurality of force sensors adapted to detect forces exerted by a caregiver, and determining from the force sensors the magnitude and direction of desired movement of the patient support apparatus. The method may also or alternatively include rotating and translating the patient support apparatus in response to the force sensors. Still further, the various methods may include determining a first magnitude and first direction of force exerted by a first caregiver on a first side of the patient support apparatus; determining a second magnitude and a second direction of force exerted by a second caregiver on a second side of the patient support apparatus; and combining the first and second magnitudes and directions to determine the magnitude and direction of desired movement of the patient support apparatus.
* [0020]

  According to the invention, a patient support apparatus is provided that includes a base, a powered wheel, a steerable wheel, a patient support deck, a force sensing system, and a controller. The force sensing system is adapted to detect both a direction and a magnitude of forces applied by a user, and it is also adapted to determine the location on the support apparatus of the applied forces relative to a reference location. The controller controls the powered wheel and the steerable wheel in a manner that takes into account the magnitude, direction, and location of the applied forces.
* [0021]

  The controller takes into account the torque or moment of force created by the applied forces based upon their location relative to a center point, center region, or other reference location. The responding movement of the support apparatus is to steer the steerable wheel in a manner that follows or matches how the patient support apparatus would turn if it were subjected to only the applied forces. That is, the controller drives the powered wheel in a manner that generally amplifies the applied forces. In some embodiments, the powered wheel and steerable wheel are the same, while in other embodiments, they are different.
* [0022]

  A patient support apparatus is dislosed that includes a base, a powered wheel, a steerable wheel, a patient support deck, a force sensing system, and a controller. The support deck includes a head end, a foot end, and a pair of sides. The force sensing system is adapted to detect both a direction and a magnitude of forces applied by a user from a first control location positioned adjacent a first one of the head end, foot end, and the sides; and the force sensing system is further adapted to detect both a direction a magnitude of forces applied by a user from a second control location positioned adjacent a second one of the head end, foot end, and the sides. The first control location is different from the second control location. The controller controls the powered wheel and the steerable wheel based upon forces detected at both the first and second control locations.
* [0023]

  In this example, the controller may be further adapted to control the powered wheel and the steerable wheel based upon forces detected simultaneously at the first and second control locations. The controller also steers the steerable wheel in a manner that follows how the patient support apparatus would turn if it were subjected to only the applied forces at either or both of the first and second control locations. The controller powers the powered wheel in a manner that generally amplifies the total applied forces at both the first and second control locations. The steerable and powered wheel may be the same wheel, or different wheels.
* [0024]

The invention may be implemented in various other embodiments and is capable of being practiced or being carried out in alternative ways not expressly disclosed herein. <u>DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE EMBODIMENTS</u>
* [0026]

  A patient support apparatus 20 according to one embodiment is shown in FIG. 1. While the particular form of patient support apparatus 20 illustrated in FIG. 1 is a bed, it will be understood that patient support apparatus 20 could, in different embodiments, be a cot, a stretcher, a gurney, or any other structure capable of supporting a patient while being transported from one place to another.
* [0027]

  In general, patient support apparatus 20 includes a base 22 having a plurality of wheels 24, a pair of elevation adjustment mechanisms 26 supported on said base, a frame or litter 28 supported on said elevation adjustment mechanisms, and a patient support deck 30 supported on said frame. Patient support apparatus 20 further includes a headboard 32 and a footboard 34.
* [0028]

  Base 22 includes a brake that is adapted to selectively lock and unlock wheels 24 so that, when unlocked, patient support apparatus 20 may be wheeled to different locations. Elevation adjustment mechanisms 26 are adapted to raise and lower frame 28 with respect to base 22. Elevation adjustment mechanisms 26 may be hydraulic actuators, electric actuators, or any other suitable device for raising and lowering frame 28 with respect to base 22. In some embodiments, elevation adjustment mechanisms 26 are operable independently so that the orientation of frame 28 with respect to base 22 can also be adjusted.
* [0029]

  Frame 28 provides a structure for supporting patient support deck 30, headboard 32, and footboard 34. Patient support deck 30 is adapted to provide a surface on which a mattress (not shown), or other soft cushion is positionable so that a patient may lie and/or sit thereon. Patient support deck 30 is made of a plurality of sections, some of which are pivotable about generally horizontal pivot axes. In the embodiment shown in FIG. 1, patient support deck 30 includes a head section 36, a seat section 38, a thigh section 40, and a foot section 42. Head section 36, which is also sometimes referred to as a Fowler section, is pivotable between a generally horizontal orientation (not shown in FIG. 1) and a plurality of raised positions (one of which is shown in FIG. 1). Thigh section 40 and foot section 42 may also be pivotable, such as is shown in FIG. 1.

  A plurality of side rails 44 (FIGS. 15-17) may also be coupled to frame 28.   FIG. 14 illustrates one example of an activation algorithm 68 used to activate or deactivate (i.e. turn on and off) the powered movement of any of the patient support apparatus embodiments disclosed herein. That is, activation algorithm controls whether or not one or more user inputs (which may be force sensors 52) will cause movement controller 50 to control one or more of either driving motors 54 or steering motors 56. When not activated, a user's manipulation of the force sensors 52, or other types of user inputs, will not result in any operation of  motors  54 and 56. When activated, a user's manipulation of force sensors 52 will cause movement controller 50 to activate one or more of  motors  54 and 56 in a manner that is dependent upon the specific user input signals that are received.
* [0054]

  In the embodiment illustrated in FIG. 14, activation algorithm 68 is partially dependent upon the presence or absence of a radio frequency (RF) identification (ID) tag worn by a clinician, or other authorized caregiver. Such RF ID tags are conventional RF ID tags that communicate with corresponding detectors or sensors when the RF ID tag is positioned within a specific vicinity of the detector or sensor. In this case, patient support apparatus 20 includes an RF ID sensor 70 (FIG. 35) that senses any authorized RF ID tags that are within a vicinity of the support apparatus 20. The vicinity boundaries may vary, but in general may be configured to only detect RF ID tags that are within the same room as patient support apparatus 20, or within a section of the same room. On some occasions, the sensor 70 may detect RF ID tags that are outside the room if they are positioned close to the doorway, but in general it is desirable to not detect tags outside of the same room or area that patient support apparatus 20 is currently located in.
* [0055]

  If activation algorithm 68 detects the presence of an RF ID tag, then control will transition to step 72. At step 72, patient support apparatus 20 monitors whether or not any user inputs are detected at either the side rails 44 of support apparatus 20, or at one of the ends of support apparatus 20 (e.g. at headboard 32 or footboard 34). If user inputs are detected at one or more of side rails 44, control passes to step 74. If user inputs are detected at either or both of headboard 32 and footboard 34, then control passes to step 76. When the control transitions to step 74, movement controller 50 will respond to detected user inputs from the side rails 44 by either implementing a translation step 78 or a steering step 80, or both, depending upon what specific inputs are detected at the side rail. If user inputs are detected only at one or both of the headboard 32 and/or footboard 34 (but not the side rails 44), then movement controller 50 will respond exclusively with steering step 80.
* [0056]

  Translation step 78 involves controlling either or both of driving motors 54 and steering motors 56 in a manner that enables support apparatus 20 to move in lateral direction 66 without any rotation. Steering step 80 involves controller either or both of driving motors 54 and steering motors 56 in a manner that will cause at least some rotation of support apparatus 20 about a generally vertical axis. Activation algorithm 68 will therefore allow only steering control when users are manipulating controls at either the head end or foot end of patient support apparatus 20, but will allow both steering and translational control when a user is manipulating controls at one or more side rails 44.

The other state is state 84, in which a user has pressed a brake button on patient support apparatus 20, or otherwise turned such a brake on. Thus, in activation algorithm 68, the brake will be activated (i.e. control will pass to braking step 86) if either no RF ID tag is detected within close proximity of support apparatus 20, or the brake is actively turned on by a user. When the brake is turned on, both  motors  54 and 56 remain off.

In other words, movement controller 50 attempts to control  motors  54 and 56 so as to mimic, but amplify, the motion of patient support 20 that would naturally occur as the result of the applied forces. In this manner, the direction and magnitude of the user's applied forces determine the movement of the support apparatus 20, but the motors 54 and/or 56 supply all or a substantial portion of the energy needed to effectuate that movement so that the user's work effort is reduced.

  In amplifying the natural movement that would result from the forces exerted by the caregiver, movement controller 50 takes into account not only the direction and magnitude of forces applies to each force sensor 52, but also the relative location of each force sensor 52 that is sensing a force. These relative positions are defined with respect to a reference location that is chosen by the manufacturer of the patient support apparatus. In some embodiments, the reference location is the geometrical center of the patient support apparatus 20, while in other embodiments the reference location is a vertical axis aligned with the center of gravity or center of mass of patient support apparatus 20, while in still other embodiments, some other reference position is used.

  Thus, for example, if a user pushes forward on footboard 34 only at position C, most of this force will be sensed by the right force sensor 52a (as shown in FIG. 15). A small amount of this forward force will also be detected by left force sensor 52a, depending upon the construction of footboard 34 and its connection to frame 28, (or even a backward force may be detected on left force sensor 52a depending upon the location of a possible pivot point of footboard 34). Regardless of what the left force sensor 52a detects, however, because the predominant force will be sensed in a forward direction at a location that is located to the right of a center 90 of patient support apparatus 20, movement controller 50 will control wheels 24 in such a manner so as to begin to turn support apparatus 20 leftward (as viewed in FIG. 15). This is because a forward force applied at location C that was greater than any forward force applied at any location on footboard 34 to the left of center point 90 would naturally (i.e. without the use of motors 54 and/or 56) tend to turn support apparatus leftward. Thus, movement controller 50 takes into account not only the direction and magnitudes of forces sensed by force sensors 52, but also takes into account where each of those force sensors 52 are located relative to a reference point, such as, but not limited to, center point 90. Stated in another way, movement controller 50 is configured to take into account the amount of torque that is applied by the sum of the sensed forces about a generally vertical axis, such as one running through center point 90, or some other point, and control motors 54 and/or 56 in a manner based on this sensed torque.

  In any of the embodiments discussed above where the patient support apparatus is configured to provide both powered translational motion and powered rotational motion, controller 50 makes the decision as to which one of, or both of, these types of movements to effectuate based upon several different factors, depending upon the specific configuration of the patient support apparatus. For example, in one embodiment, any detected force inputs from force sensors 52 will result in controller 50 causing purely translational motion of the support apparatus if the speed sensor(s) indicates that the support apparatus is currently traveling under a threshold speed. If the support apparatus is currently traveling at a speed equal to, or faster than, the threshold speed, then any forces detected by force sensors 52 will be processed by controller 50 in a manner that causes powered rotation of the support apparatus to occur. The current speed of the patient support apparatus may alternatively be used in different manners to control whether translational or rotational motion is applied.

In other words, while the support apparatus is below the threshold speed, controller 50 supplies power to the motors 54 and/or 56 in any manner (lateral translation, longitudinal translation, and/or clockwise or counterclockwise rotation), depending upon the forces applied by a user to force sensors 52.   In one embodiment, controller 50 will direct motors 54 and/or 56 to generate a purely lateral translation of support apparatus 20 only when the one or more force sensors 52 detect forces in the lateral direction (e.g. 66 of FIG. 15). In this embodiment, the controller 50 directs motors 54 and/or 56 to provide longitudinal power when the magnitude and direction of forces applied to at least two force sensors 52 are the same, or have nearly the same direction and nearly the same magnitude. Further, in this embodiment, the controller 50 directs motors 54 and/or 56 to rotate the support apparatus based upon the difference, if any, in the magnitude and/or direction of forces applied to the two or more force sensors 52. Thus, for example, if a caregiver pushes forward on a pair of force sensors 52 with generally the same magnitude, controller 50 directs motors 54 and/or 56 to longitudinally translate the support apparatus forward without rotation. If a caregiver pushes forward on one force sensor 52 and pulls backward on the other force sensor 52, controller 50 directs motors 54 and/or 56 to rotate the support apparatus without either longitudinal or lateral translation (and the direction of rotation will depend upon which force sensor is pushed forward and which is pulled backward). If the caregiver applies a purely lateral force to one or both of the force sensors 52, then controller 50 directs motors 54 and/or 56 to effect a purely lateral translation of the patient support apparatus. Further, if mixtures of these forces are applied, controller 50 applies the appropriate combination of translation and rotation. Thus, for example, if a caregiver pushes forward on both force sensors 52 but with magnitudes of force that are different from each other by more than a threshold amount, controller 50 controls motors 54 and/or 56 to apply both a forward longitudinal translation and some amount of rotation-the amount being dependent upon the degree of difference in the magnitude of the applied forces.
